messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 64

Elias, a fifty-five-year-old African man who has spent his life reading terrain, sits on the edge of his kitchen chair, fingers tracing the rim of a cold mug. The rain taps against the window, a steady rhythm that makes his shoulders draw up toward his ears. He remembers the day the river broke. He was on the north span, checking the floodgates, when the water stopped behaving like water and became a wall. The siren from the command center cut through the roar, but he was already wading, boots heavy with silt, pulling strangers toward higher ground. His wife, Amara, called him that night. Her voice was thin, frayed at the edges. “Elias, come home. Just come home.” He did, but the river had already taken the lower ward. The water receded, but the silence it left behind never did. For months after, he couldn’t stay in the house. He drove the perimeter roads, watching for cracks in the asphalt, listening for the hum of strained wires. The city reassured him the ground was stable, but his skin kept telling him otherwise. He works as a bomb disposal technician now, yet the architecture of his mind never adjusted to the suddenness of the flood. He still calls it “clearing the site” in his head. Every rusted hinge, every snapped power line, triggers the same cold sweep in his chest. He walks past the flooded neighborhoods with his jaw locked, counting his steps. Three, four, five. Anything to keep the images from spilling over. When he closes his eyes, he sees the way the current dragged a child’s red rain boot under the overpass. He wakes at 3 a.m. most nights, heart hammering, palms slick, convinced the ceiling is bowing from pressure. He doesn’t call for Amara. He just lies there, listening to the house settle, telling himself it’s only the foundation. Amara tries. She leaves his favorite stew on the stove and walks on the rug, though he hasn’t told her he can hear her footsteps like distant detonations. She notices how he flinches when the dishwasher cycles, how he scans the perimeter before he sits at the table. He loves her, fiercely, but love feels like a bridge he’s trying to cross with numb fingers. He kisses her forehead at night, murmurs that everything’s fine, and turns his face to the wall. The guilt sits in his ribs like a stone he swallowed with the floodwater. He should have reached her cousin. He should have stayed on the line longer. His training told him to assess, to control, to neutralize. None of it mattered when the earth just gave way. On weekends, he takes his truck to the edge of the new levee system, kills the engine, and sits in the cab. The rain has stopped, but the smell of wet concrete and damp soil clings to the windows. He watches the water move, slow and heavy, and wonders if it’s still angry. His hands rest on his knees, palms up, exactly as he was taught to clear a trigger mechanism. He breathes in. He breathes out. The numbers in his head keep time. He doesn’t know when it will stop, but he keeps coming back, again and again, to sit in the quiet and listen to the water, waiting for the moment it finally lets him rest.
